structure.summary:
- Company identity and scope: General Mills, Inc., incorporated in Delaware in 1928, is a leading global manufacturer and marketer of branded consumer foods and wholesome natural pet food, with products made in 13 countries and sold in 100+ countries. It also supplies branded and unbranded products to North American foodservice and commercial baking.
- Joint ventures: Holds 50% interests in two strategic JVs—Cereal Partners Worldwide (with Nestlé) for ready-to-eat cereal outside North America, and Häagen-Dazs Japan for super-premium ice cream in Japan—selling in 130+ countries.
- Operating segments: Five segments—North America Retail; Convenience Stores & Foodservice; Europe & Australia; Asia & Latin America; and Pet. The Pet segment reported 13 months in fiscal 2020 due to a fiscal-year alignment change; fiscal 2019 included 12 months; fiscal 2018 excluded Pet.
- Product categories: Focus on large global categories including snacks; ready-to-eat cereal; convenient meals (meal kits, ethnic meals, pizza, soup, sides, frozen breakfast, frozen entrées); yogurt; wholesome natural pet food; super-premium ice cream; baking mixes/ingredients; and refrigerated/frozen dough.
- Customers and channels: Sells primarily to grocery, mass merchandisers, membership clubs, natural food chains, drug/dollar/discount chains, e-commerce retailers, foodservice distributors/operators, restaurants, convenience stores, and pet specialty stores, mainly via a direct sales force with some broker/distributor arrangements.
- Customer concentration: Walmart accounted for 21% of consolidated net sales and 30% of North America Retail net sales in fiscal 2020; no other customer reached 10% of consolidated net sales.
- Competitive environment: Highly competitive packaged and pet food markets globally, with competition from large manufacturers and retailer private brands across brick-and-mortar and e-commerce; key competitive factors include product innovation, quality, price, and brand recognition/loyalty.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1 Business
structure.start_phrase: General Mills, Inc. was incorporated in Delaware in 1928.
structure.summary:
- Company overview: General Mills is a leading global manufacturer and marketer of branded consumer foods and natural pet food, operating manufacturing in 13 countries and marketing in 100+ countries. It holds 50% interests in two major JVs: Cereal Partners Worldwide (with Nestlé) and Häagen-Dazs Japan. The Pet segment had 13 months of results in fiscal 2020 due to a reporting calendar change.
- Operating segments: North America Retail; Convenience Stores & Foodservice; Europe & Australia; Asia & Latin America; and Pet.
- Product categories: snacks; ready-to-eat cereal; convenient meals (meal kits, pizza, soup, sides, frozen breakfast/entrées); yogurt; wholesome natural pet food; super-premium ice cream; baking mixes/ingredients; refrigerated and frozen dough.
- Customers and sales channels: Grocery, mass merchandisers, club, natural, drug/dollar/discount chains, e-commerce, foodservice distributors/operators, restaurants, convenience, and pet specialty; primarily direct sales with some broker/distributor arrangements. Walmart represented 21% of consolidated net sales and 30% of North America Retail sales in fiscal 2020.
- Competition: Highly competitive categories globally, including branded, regional, private label, and retailer brands across brick-and-mortar and e-commerce. Key competitive factors include innovation, quality, price, brand strength, marketing, promotion, convenience, and consumer insight. Strategies emphasize insights, customer relationships, quality, advertising, innovation, supply chain efficiency, and pricing.
- Raw materials and packaging: Major inputs include grains, dairy, sugar, oils, meats, nuts, fruits/vegetables, and packaging (carton, corrugated, plastic, metal), plus energy. Costs can fluctuate due to weather, climate change, scarcity, commodity/currency volatility, tariffs, pandemics (including COVID-19), and policy/regulatory changes. Mix of open-market purchasing and some fixed-price contracts; risk managed with various strategies and a grain merchandising operation using derivatives.
- Research and development: Focus on new products, improvements, process and packaging innovation, and exploratory research; R&D spend was $224 million in fiscal 2020 and $222 million in fiscal 2019.
- Trademarks and patents: Portfolio includes major global brands (e.g., Annie’s, Betty Crocker, Blue Buffalo, Cheerios, Häagen-Dazs, Nature Valley, Old El Paso, Pillsbury, Progresso, Yoplait). Various licensing arrangements (e.g., CPW cereal marks; Häagen-Dazs licensed to Nestlé in U.S./Canada and to HDJ; Pillsbury mixes licensed to a third party; Yoplait/Liberté trademark ownership and licensing structure). Patents are valuable collectively but not individually material.
- Seasonality: Overall demand is balanced annually, with higher fourth-quarter demand for refrigerated dough, frozen baked goods, and baking products; Progresso soup peaks in fall/winter; Häagen-Dazs ice cream peaks in summer; baking/dough rise in winter internationally, with offsetting hemispheric seasonality.
- Backlog: Orders typically filled within days and cancellable pre-shipment. COVID-19 drove elevated retail demand in Q4 fiscal 2020; production was ramped and prioritized, yet some orders could not be fulfilled.
- Working capital and returns: Working capital discussed in MD&A; product return practices in financial statement notes.
- Employees: Approximately 35,000 as of May 31, 2020.
- Regulation: Operations subject to extensive U.S. and international food and pet food safety, advertising, environmental, and related regulations.
- Environmental matters: Involved in two response actions (Minneapolis, MN; Moonachie, NJ). Subject to major environmental statutes; compliance and proceedings not expected to have a material adverse effect.
- Executive leadership: Listing and backgrounds of key executive officers, including CEO/Chairman Jeffrey L. Harmening and leaders across finance, supply chain, segments, IT, marketing, HR, legal, and accounting.
- Website access: SEC filings and ownership reports available on GeneralMills.com and SEC.gov.
- Risk factors (partial):
  - COVID-19 impacts: Potential adverse effects from reduced away-from-home sales; macroeconomic deterioration; workforce and supply chain disruptions; demand volatility and capacity constraints; third-party partner failures; political/regulatory restrictions; and potential investigations/litigation stemming from pandemic-related actions.
  - Competitive risks: Intense competition from branded and private label players; pricing/promotional dynamics that may pressure margins, revenue, and market share.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: Our business is subject to various risks and uncertainties.
structure.summary:
- Item 1A – Risk Factors: Broad set of risks that could materially affect business, financial condition, and results of operations.
  - COVID-19 impacts: lower sales in away-from-home channels; demand volatility; economic downturn (unemployment, reduced disposable income); workforce and supply chain disruptions despite safety measures; production constraints and unfilled orders; third-party failures; government restrictions; potential investigations/litigation.
  - Competitive pressures: intense competition from global brands and private label; need for innovation, quality, pricing, and effective marketing/e-commerce; risk to margins from price/promotional activity; brand equity needed to sustain premium pricing; retail consolidation increasing customer bargaining power and private label emphasis; customer concentration risk (e.g., Walmart significance).
  - Input cost and financial volatility: commodity, packaging, and energy price fluctuations; partial hedging and derivative-related earnings volatility; grain inventories at net realizable value; potential margin compression if costs outpace pricing/productivity.
  - Operational efficiency and restructuring: execution risks in productivity initiatives, manufacturing realignments, and cost savings programs; potential production interruptions and missed benefits.
  - Supply chain vulnerabilities: disruptions from weather, climate change, disasters, cyber-attacks, pandemics, strikes, regulations, and single-source dependencies; supplier disputes and practices affecting quality/reputation.
  - Product safety and quality: consumer confidence risks; recalls, product liability, and reputational damage if products are adulterated, misbranded, or mislabeled.
  - Shifts in consumer preferences: need to anticipate tastes, channels (including e-commerce), and health concerns (e.g., sodium, trans fats, GMOs, sugar, processed wheat, grain-free/legume-rich pet foods); risk of reduced demand if trends are missed.
  - Growth and market share: constrained category growth; importance of innovation and entry into faster-growing, higher-margin categories.
  - Macroeconomic risks: economic downturns driving trade-down to lower-margin offerings and reduced away-from-home consumption; pricing power constraints.
  - Brand reputation: dependence on maintaining strong brand perception; rapid amplification of negative information via social/digital media.
  - International exposure: political/economic instability, FX fluctuations (and USD strength), tariffs, nationalization, anti-corruption compliance, Brexit uncertainty, tax and fund transfer restrictions; limited effectiveness of currency hedges.
  - Regulatory and legal environment: compliance with USDA, FDA, OSHA, and other regulations on food safety, labeling, worker safety; advertising and marketing restrictions/claims risk; environmental laws and remediation obligations with potential cost variability; COVID-19-related governmental actions affecting operations.
  - Capital structure and liquidity: substantial indebtedness and covenant constraints; potential ratings pressure limiting financing flexibility; capital market volatility (exacerbated by COVID-19) affecting liquidity and borrowing costs; counterparty risk; IBOR transition uncertainties.
  - Employee benefit plans: pension/OPEB cost and funding volatility due to interest rates, mortality, investment returns, and asset values.
  - Information technology and cybersecurity: dependence on IT systems (including third parties); risks from outages, breaches, and data loss leading to operational, legal, and financial impacts.
  - Goodwill and intangible assets: significant balances subject to impairment testing; sensitivity to growth, discount rate, and macro assumptions; monitoring underperforming units/brands (e.g., Europe & Australia reporting unit; Pillsbury, Progresso).
  - M&A execution: integration risks, increased leverage, potential loss of key people/customers, unknown liabilities, synergy shortfalls, and possible asset impairments.

- Item 1B – Unresolved Staff Comments: None.

- Item 2 – Properties: Overview of owned headquarters and R&D in Minneapolis; global footprint of operations.
  - 47 manufacturing facilities as of May 31, 2020: 24 U.S. (1 leased), 4 Greater China, 1 Asia/Middle East/Africa, 2 Canada (1 leased), 8 Europe/Australia, 8 Latin America/Mexico.
  - Principal production facilities listed by segment (North America Retail; Convenience Stores & Foodservice; Europe & Australia; Asia & Latin America; Pet) with key locations across the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Europe, Australia, Brazil, China, and India.
  - Additional assets: numerous U.S. grain elevators; ~15 million sq ft of largely leased warehouse/distribution space (primarily for North America Retail); ~3 million sq ft of owned/leased sales and administrative offices; additional on-site warehouse/distribution/office space.
  - Häagen-Dazs retail: 500 company-operated (all leased) and 358 franchised branded ice cream parlors outside the U.S. and Canada.

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7 Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase: We are a global packaged foods company.
structure.summary:
- Executive overview of a global packaged foods company’s strategy and long-term financial goals, emphasizing brand building, innovation, and balanced growth in sales, margins, cash conversion, and shareholder returns.
- Fiscal 2020 performance highlights: net sales of $17.6 billion (+5%; organic +4%), operating profit up 17%, adjusted operating profit up 7% on a constant-currency basis, diluted EPS $3.56 (+23%), adjusted diluted EPS $3.61 (+12% constant currency), and strong free cash flow of $3.2 billion with robust conversion.
- COVID-19 impact analysis: sharp increase in at-home food demand boosting North America Retail and Pet (stock-up effects), with headwinds in away-from-home channels affecting Convenience Stores & Foodservice and Asia & Latin America; Europe & Australia modestly affected. Approximately 3 points of net sales and organic net sales growth attributed to pandemic-related demand.
- Execution against three FY20 priorities: accelerated organic net sales growth (notably in meals, baking, cereal, and Blue Buffalo Pet expansion), maintained strong adjusted operating profit margins via HMM savings, positive price/mix and volume, and reduced leverage through disciplined cash management.
- FY21 priorities and outlook: compete effectively to drive penetration and share; drive efficiency to fund investment; further reduce leverage. Expect elevated at-home demand vs. pre-pandemic, with uncertainties tied to restaurant reopening, work-from-home, schools, and macro conditions; anticipate FY21 adjusted operating profit margin roughly in line with FY20 and sales headwinds from 53rd week, extra Pet month, and lapping Q4 FY20 surge.
- Consolidated results detail: 53-week FY20 vs. 52-week FY19; Pet segment aligned to fiscal calendar (13 months in FY20). Gross margin up 70 bps to 34.8%; SG&A up $216 million (higher compensation/benefits and media), effective tax rate 18.5% (adjusted 20.7%), lower net interest expense, higher JV after-tax earnings (notably CPW).
- Segment performance:
  - North America Retail: net sales +8% (organic +6%), led by Meals & Baking and U.S. Cereal; segment operating profit +15%.
  - Europe & Australia: net sales -3% (FX headwind), organic -1%; operating profit -8% (higher input costs, lower volumes).
  - Convenience Stores & Foodservice: net sales -8% (volume and price/mix declines from COVID-19), operating profit -20%.
  - Pet: net sales +18% (volume-led, including extra month; favorable price/mix; COVID-19 boost), operating profit +46%.
  - Asia & Latin America: net sales -8% (FX, volume, price/mix; COVID-19), operating profit -74%.
- Liquidity and cash flows: operating cash flow $3.7 billion (+$869 million YoY), capex $461 million, dividends $1.196 billion, minimal share repurchases, net debt reduced by ~$1.0 billion; strong access to liquidity via $2.9 billion committed credit facilities (undrawn) and commercial paper programs.
- Capital structure and resources: total debt $13.54 billion; net debt-to-operating cash flow 3.2; net debt-to-adjusted EBITDA 3.2 (improved from 3.9); increased fixed-rate debt mix; covenant compliance; schedule of upcoming maturities and ample liquidity to meet near-term obligations.
- Inflation and cost management: experienced ~4% input cost inflation in FY20; expect ~3% in FY21; continued HMM initiatives and risk management of commodities and currencies.
- Significant accounting estimates and policies: revenue recognition (trade promotions/coupons), long-lived asset impairment testing, goodwill and brand intangibles (no FY20 impairments; monitoring Europe & Australia reporting unit and Progresso brand; Pillsbury coverage noted), redeemable interest valuation, stock-based compensation assumptions, income tax uncertainties, and pension/OPEB assumptions (lower expected asset returns, discount rate sensitivities, healthcare trend rates).
- Contractual obligations and off-balance-sheet items: detailed table of debt, leases, and purchase commitments; limited guarantees and VIE exposure; defined benefit funding status and PPA considerations.
- Non-GAAP measures and reconciliations: definitions and detailed bridges for organic net sales, adjusted diluted EPS (and constant-currency growth), adjusted operating profit/margins (and constant-currency growth), free cash flow conversion, constant-currency JV earnings growth, Canada constant-currency sales, and net debt-to-adjusted EBITDA.
- Risk and forward-looking statements: comprehensive safe harbor discussion outlining key uncertainties (COVID-19 trajectory, supply chain, competition, costs, consumer trends, FX, interest rates, regulatory changes, IT/security, and geopolitical factors).
- Market risk disclosures: qualitative and quantitative (VAR) assessments of interest rate, FX, commodity, and equity exposures, hedging practices, and methodology used for VAR estimation.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase: We are exposed to market risk stemming from changes in interest and foreign exchange rates and commodity and equity prices.
structure.summary:
- Forward-looking statements and safe harbor: Identifies numerous factors that could materially affect future results and cause variances from current expectations, including COVID-19 impacts; supply chain disruptions; competitive activity (new products, advertising, pricing, promotion); macroeconomic conditions (inflation, interest and tax rates, capital availability); product development and consumer acceptance; pricing/promotion elasticity; M&A and capital structure changes; legal/regulatory shifts (tax, labeling/advertising, litigation); impairments and accounting changes; product quality/safety and recalls; shifts in consumer demand and health-related perceptions (including obesity and weight-loss trends); retail consolidation and customer inventory levels; volatility and availability of raw materials, packaging, and energy; effectiveness of restructuring/cost-savings; derivative market value volatility; benefit plan expense drivers; IT system failures/breaches; foreign economic/currency risks; and geopolitical risks (unrest, terrorism, war). References Item 1A risk factors and disclaims obligation to update forward-looking statements.

- Market risk management (Item 7A): Company is exposed to interest rate, foreign exchange, commodity, and equity price risks; manages exposure via hedging under established policies with highly rated counterparties and credit limits, using various derivatives. Additional details referenced in Note 8 to the financial statements.

- Value at Risk (VaR) methodology: Monte Carlo VaR with a 95% confidence level using past-year RiskMetrics data under normal market conditions to estimate 1-day maximum potential fair value loss. Notes that hedge instruments generally offset underlying exposures. Positions included debt, investments, interest rate swaps, FX forwards, commodity swaps/futures/options, and equity instruments; underlying exposures offset by these instruments are not included.

- VaR results (fair value impact, in millions):
  - Interest rate instruments: $78.8 (May 31, 2020); average FY2020 $80.3; $74.4 (May 26, 2019)
  - Foreign currency instruments: $19.3; average $15.3; $16.8 (2019)
  - Commodity instruments: $2.6; average $3.0; $4.1 (2019)

- Context: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements for General Mills, Inc. and Subsidiaries, covering Basis of Presentation and Significant Accounting Policies.
- Basis of presentation:
  - Consolidation of entities where the company has a controlling financial interest; elimination of intercompany transactions, including portions attributable to noncontrolling and redeemable interests.
  - Fiscal year ends on the last Sunday in May; FY2020 had 53 weeks vs. 52 weeks in FY2019 and FY2018.
  - Certain prior-period reclassifications to conform with current presentation (see Note 2).
  - Change in reporting period: Pet segment moved from April to May year-end in FY2020; FY2020 includes 13 months of Pet results; impact not material, no restatement. India business operates on an April fiscal year-end.
- Significant accounting policies:
  - Cash and cash equivalents: investments with original maturities of three months or less.
  - Inventories:
    - U.S. (non-grain): lower of cost (LIFO) or market.
    - Grain: net realizable value; related cash contracts and derivatives at fair value with changes recognized in earnings.
    - Outside U.S.: generally lower of cost (FIFO) or net realizable value.
    - Shipping costs to customers recorded in cost of sales and recognized when product is shipped and accepted.
  - Land, buildings, equipment, and depreciation:
    - Land at historical cost; buildings/equipment at cost (including capitalized interest and internal engineering) and depreciated primarily straight-line.
    - Typical useful lives: buildings ~40 years; equipment/furniture/software 3–10 years.
    - Maintenance and repairs expensed; fully depreciated assets retained until disposal; gains/losses recognized upon sale or retirement.
    - Assets held for sale were insignificant as of May 31, 2020.
  - Long-lived asset impairment:
    - Tested upon indicators; impairment if undiscounted cash flows of the asset group are less than carrying amount.
    - Loss measured as excess of carrying amount over fair value (via discounted cash flows or independent appraisals); asset groups have identifiable, largely independent cash flows.
  - Goodwill and other intangible assets:
    - Goodwill not amortized; tested annually (first day of fiscal Q2) and upon triggering events.
    - Testing by reporting unit by comparing carrying value (including goodwill) to fair value.

nodes.title: Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets
nodes.heading: Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets
nodes.start_phrase: Goodwill is not subject to amortization and is tested for impairment annually and whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that impairment may have occurred.
nodes.summary:
- Basis of presentation: Consolidates General Mills, Inc. and controlled subsidiaries; eliminates intercompany transactions, including noncontrolling and redeemable interests. Fiscal year ends last Sunday in May; FY2020 had 53 weeks (vs. 52 in FY2019 and FY2018). Certain prior-period reclassifications made. Reporting period change: Pet segment moved from April to May year-end in FY2020 (13 months of results; impact not material); India business remains on an April year-end.

- Significant accounting policies:
  - Cash equivalents: Investments with original maturities of three months or less.
  - Inventories: U.S. non-grain at lower of cost (LIFO) or market; grain at net realizable value with related cash contracts/derivatives at fair value through earnings; non-U.S. generally lower of cost (FIFO) or net realizable value. Shipping costs to customers recorded in cost of sales when product is shipped and accepted.
  - Property, plant, and equipment: Land at historical cost; buildings/equipment at cost (including capitalized interest and internal engineering) depreciated straight-line (buildings ~40 years; equipment/furniture/software ~3–10 years). Maintenance charged to cost of sales. Disposal gains/losses recognized on retirement/sale; assets held for sale insignificant at May 31, 2020. Long-lived asset impairment: test when indicators arise; compare undiscounted cash flows to carrying amount; measure impairment using fair value (DCF or appraisal).
  - Goodwill and other intangibles: Goodwill not amortized; annual impairment test as of day one of fiscal Q2 or upon indicators, at reporting-unit level using DCF; recognize impairment up to carrying amount of goodwill. Intangible lives assessed as finite or indefinite. Finite-lived intangibles (e.g., franchise agreements, customer relationships) amortized straight-line over ~4–30 years; impairment testing similar to long-lived assets. Indefinite-lived brands (e.g., Blue Buffalo, Pillsbury, Totino’s, Yoplait, Old El Paso, Progresso, Annie’s, Häagen-Dazs, Yoki) tested annually or upon indicators; fair value estimated via DCF using projected revenues, assumed royalty rates, and discount rate.
  - Leases: Identify leases at inception; separate lease and non-lease components based on relative standalone prices. Short-term leases (12 months or less) not capitalized; expense straight-line. Include renewal/termination options when reasonably certain. Variable rentals (e.g., sales-based Häagen-Dazs shop rents, inflation-indexed adjustments) excluded from lease liabilities and expensed as incurred. Incremental borrowing rate used to discount lease payments where no implicit rate exists.
  - Investments in unconsolidated joint ventures: Equity method accounting (cost plus share of undistributed earnings/losses). Company may earn royalties, incur expenses (primarily R&D), and record certain tax impacts; may provide loans/capital and sell materials/goods to JVs at market prices. Impairment assessed upon indicators (e.g., operating losses, lower projections, higher WACC, significant disruptions); fair value estimates consider growth, profitability, royalty rates, capex, depreciation, taxes, FX, and discount rate; write-downs recognized if declines are other than temporary.

nodes.title: Leases
nodes.heading: Leases
nodes.start_phrase: We determine whether an arrangement is a lease at inception.
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill impairment testing is performed at the reporting unit level annually or when triggering events occur. Fair value is estimated using a discounted cash flow model incorporating long-range plan growth rates, discount rates, perpetuity growth, market comparables, and other factors. Any impairment is recognized up to the amount of goodwill allocated to the unit.
- Intangible assets’ useful lives are evaluated to determine whether they are finite or indefinite, based on judgments about obsolescence, demand, competition, regulatory environment, required maintenance, and related asset lives. Finite-lived intangibles are amortized straight-line over 4–30 years.
- Indefinite-lived brand intangibles (including Blue Buffalo, Pillsbury, Totino’s, Yoplait, Old El Paso, Progresso, Annie’s, Häagen-Dazs, and Yoki) are tested annually and upon triggering events. Fair value is estimated using a relief-from-royalty discounted cash flow model with projected revenues, assumed royalty rates, and a discount rate.
- Finite-lived intangibles (e.g., franchise agreements and customer relationships) are tested for impairment upon triggering events using an undiscounted cash flow recoverability test; if not recoverable, the loss is measured as the excess of carrying value over fair value, typically via a discounted cash flow model.
- Lease accounting: arrangements are identified at inception and lease/non-lease components are separated based on relative standalone prices. Short-term leases (12 months or less) are not recorded on the balance sheet and are expensed straight-line. Renewal/termination options are included in the lease term when reasonably certain. Contracts generally lack purchase options, residual guarantees, or restrictive covenants.
- Variable lease payments (e.g., percentage rents for Häagen-Dazs shops or index-based adjustments) are excluded from lease liabilities and recognized as incurred due to their uncertainty.
- Because most leases lack an implicit rate, an incremental borrowing rate at commencement is used to discount lease payments.
- Investments in unconsolidated joint ventures are accounted for under the equity method. The company earns royalties, incurs certain expenses (notably R&D), records tax impacts for partnership-structured JVs, provides loans/capital, and sells materials and goods to JVs at market prices.
- JV investments are assessed for impairment upon indicators such as operating losses, reduced earnings outlook, higher weighted-average cost of capital, or significant disruptions. Fair value estimates consider revenue growth, profitability, royalty rates, capital spending, depreciation, taxes, foreign exchange, and discount rates; if carrying value exceeds fair value, the company evaluates whether the decline is temporary or other-than-temporary for potential write-down.

nodes.title: Investments in Unconsolidated Joint Ventures
nodes.heading: Investments in Unconsolidated Joint Ventures
nodes.start_phrase: Our investments in companies over which we have the ability to exercise significant influence are stated at cost plus our share of undistributed earnings or losses.
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill: Annual and trigger-based impairment testing at the reporting unit level using discounted cash flow (DCF) valuations; impairment recognized to the extent carrying value exceeds fair value, limited to recorded goodwill. Key assumptions include revenue/profit growth, discount rates, perpetuity growth, market comparables, and other factors.
- Intangible assets: Assessment of finite vs. indefinite lives based on judgments about obsolescence, demand, competition, regulation, maintenance, and related asset lives. Finite-lived intangibles amortized straight-line over 4–30 years.
- Indefinite-lived brands: Annual and trigger-based impairment testing of major brands (e.g., Blue Buffalo, Pillsbury, Totino’s, Yoplait, Old El Paso, Progresso, Annie’s, Häagen-Dazs, Yoki) using DCF with projected revenues, assumed royalty rates, and discount rates.
- Finite-lived intangibles (e.g., franchise agreements, customer relationships): Impairment testing upon indicators; recoverability based on undiscounted cash flows; impairment measured by excess of carrying amount over fair value (DCF or similar).
- Leases: Identification at inception; separation of lease and non-lease components; short-term leases expensed straight-line and not capitalized; lease term includes reasonably certain renewals/terminations; variable rents (e.g., sales-based or index-linked) expensed as incurred; incremental borrowing rate used when no implicit rate.
- Investments in unconsolidated joint ventures: Equity method accounting; company may receive royalties, incur certain expenses, recognize partnership tax impacts, provide loans/capital, and transact sales at market prices. Impairment assessments consider operating performance, WACC, disruptions, and DCF assumptions (growth, margins, royalty rates, capex, FX, discount rate); write-downs if other-than-temporary.
- Redeemable interest: 49% interest in Yoplait SAS held by Sodiaal classified outside equity due to put option exercisable up to three times before Dec 2024; remeasured quarterly to redemption (fair) value through additional paid-in capital; reclassified to noncontrolling interests when put lapses. Valuation based on long-range plan, capex, depreciation, taxes, FX, discount rate.
- Revenue recognition: Contracts generally short-term with a single performance obligation; revenue recognized at transfer of control (typically customer acceptance of shipment). Sales include billed shipping/handling and are net of variable consideration (trade promotions, coupons, returns/unsaleables, prompt-pay discounts). Significant judgment in estimating promotions; updates recognized as changes in estimate. Limited returns; receivables generally non-interest-bearing, short-term; allowance for doubtful accounts recorded. No material contract assets/liabilities; revenue disaggregation referenced in Note 17.
- Environmental costs: Past-condition costs expensed; remediation liabilities recorded undiscounted when probable and reasonably estimable.
- Advertising: Production costs expensed upon first run.
- Research and development: Expensed as incurred; includes product/process innovation costs, primarily internal labor, consulting, supplies, plus facility depreciation/maintenance (including pilot plants).
- Foreign currency: Local currency as functional for significant foreign operations; assets/liabilities translated at period-end rates, income at average rates; translation adjustments to AOCI. Transaction gains/losses in earnings except for net investment hedges and certain long-term investments, which go to AOCI.
- Derivative instruments: Recorded at fair value in current/noncurrent assets or liabilities; changes recognized in earnings or OCI based on hedge designation and effectiveness, with amounts in AOCI reclassified per hedge accounting rules.

nodes.title: Redeemable Interest
nodes.heading: Redeemable Interest
nodes.start_phrase: We have a 51 percent controlling interest in Yoplait SAS, a consolidated entity.
nodes.summary:
- Investment impairment: write down to fair value when impairment is other than temporary.
- Redeemable noncontrolling interest (Yoplait SAS): Sodiaal’s 49% interest includes a put option exercisable up to three times before December 2024; classified outside equity while exercisable and reclassified to noncontrolling interests once no longer exercisable. Redemption value (approximate fair value) adjusted quarterly through additional paid-in capital using assumptions for growth, profitability, capex, depreciation, taxes, FX, and discount rate.
- Revenue recognition: single performance obligation (delivery of product); revenue recognized at point in time when control transfers (generally upon customer acceptance). Sales reported net of variable consideration and consideration payable (trade promotions, coupons, returns/unsalable allowances, prompt-pay discounts); excludes sales and similar taxes. Significant judgment for trade promotion estimates; changes recognized in subsequent periods. Limited, pre-approved returns; receivables non-interest-bearing with short-term terms and no significant financing components. Allowance for doubtful accounts based on past due and specific account data; write-offs when uncollectible. No material contract assets or liabilities; revenue disaggregation referenced in Note 17.
- Environmental costs: expense legacy environmental costs; record undiscounted remediation liabilities when probable and reasonably estimable.
- Advertising: expense production costs when first run.
- Research and development: expense as incurred; primarily salaries, consulting, supplies; includes depreciation and maintenance of R&D and pilot plant facilities.
- Foreign currency: local currency as functional for significant foreign operations; balance sheets translated at period-end rates, income statements at average rates; translation adjustments in AOCI. FX transaction gains/losses in earnings except for long-term investments in subsidiaries and net investment hedges, which go to AOCI.
- Derivatives: recognized at fair value in current/noncurrent assets or liabilities based on maturity; changes in fair value recorded in earnings or other comprehensive income depending on hedge designation, with AOCI amounts reclassified per hedge accounting rules.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition
nodes.heading: Revenue Recognition
nodes.start_phrase: Our revenues primarily result from contracts with customers, which are generally short-term and have a single performance obligation – the delivery of product.
nodes.summary:
- Investment impairment: Write down investments to fair value when impairments are deemed other than temporary.
- Redeemable interest (Yoplait SAS): Company holds 51% controlling stake; Sodiaal owns 49% with a put option exercisable once per year up to three times before December 2024. Because the put is exercisable, Sodiaal’s interest is classified outside equity as a redeemable interest; it will be reclassified to noncontrolling interests when the put expires. The redemption value (approximating fair value) is adjusted quarterly through additional paid-in capital, based on assumptions including long-range revenue/profit outlook, capex, depreciation, taxes, FX rates, and discount rate.
- Revenue recognition: Contracts generally have a single performance obligation (product delivery). Revenue is recognized at the point control transfers, typically upon customer acceptance of shipment. Sales include billed shipping/handling and are presented net of variable consideration and amounts payable to customers (trade promotions, coupons, returns/unsalable allowances, prompt-pay discounts). Sales and similar taxes are excluded. Trade promotion estimates involve significant judgment and are trued up as changes in estimate. Returns are generally not allowed except in limited, preapproved cases; saleable returns may be resold. Receivables are non-interest-bearing with short-term terms; no significant financing component. Allowance for doubtful accounts is based on past dues and specific account data; write-offs occur when uncollectible. No material contract assets or liabilities; revenue disaggregation is provided elsewhere (Note 17).
- Environmental costs: Costs tied to past operations that don’t benefit current/future revenues are expensed. Remediation liabilities are recorded on an undiscounted basis when probable and reasonably estimable, typically by feasibility study completion or commitment to an action plan.
- Advertising: Production costs are expensed the first time the advertising runs.
- Research and development: All R&D costs are expensed as incurred, including internal labor, consulting, supplies, and depreciation/maintenance of R&D and pilot plant facilities.
- Foreign currency: Functional currency for significant foreign operations is the local currency. Assets/liabilities translated at period-end rates; income statement at average rates. Translation adjustments go to AOCI. Transaction gains/losses go to net earnings, except for certain net investment-related items and designated net investment hedges, which go to AOCI.
- Derivatives: All derivatives are recognized at fair value as current or noncurrent assets/liabilities based on maturity. Fair value changes go to net earnings or other comprehensive income depending on hedge designation/effectiveness; amounts in AOCI are reclassified out when appropriate.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments
nodes.heading: Derivative Instruments
nodes.start_phrase: All derivatives are recognized on our Consolidated Balance Sheets at fair value based on quoted market prices or our estimate of their fair value, and are recorded in either current or noncurrent assets or liabilities based on their maturity.
nodes.summary:
- Impairment of investments: write down to fair value if impairment is deemed other than temporary.
- Redeemable interest in Yoplait SAS: Company holds 51% controlling stake; Sodiaal holds 49% with an annual put option exercisable up to three times before December 2024. Sodiaal’s interest classified outside equity while put is exercisable; reclassified to noncontrolling interests once it expires. Redemption value (approximate fair value) adjusted quarterly through additional paid-in capital using assumptions on growth, profitability, capex, depreciation, taxes, FX, and discount rate.
- Revenue recognition: Contracts generally short-term with a single performance obligation (product delivery). Revenue recognized at customer acceptance; sales include shipping/handling billed and are net of variable consideration (trade promotions, coupons, returns, unsalable product, prompt-pay). Taxes excluded. Limited return rights. No significant financing components. Allowance for doubtful accounts based on past-due and specific data. No material contract assets or liabilities; revenue disaggregated in Note 17.

nodes.title: Stock-based Compensation
nodes.heading: Stock-based Compensation
nodes.start_phrase: We generally measure compensation expense for grants of restricted stock units and performance share units using the value of a share of our stock on the date of grant.
nodes.summary:
- Hedge accounting: Amounts recorded in AOCI for hedges are reclassified to earnings when the underlying hedged transaction ceases to exist.
- Stock-based compensation: RSUs/PSUs measured at grant-date stock price; options valued with Black-Scholes; expense recognized straight-line over vesting, recorded in SG&A and cost of sales and allocated to segments. Awards with retirement/termination/death provisions may vest sooner; compensation for retirement-eligible participants is recognized immediately or up to the eligibility date. Excess tax benefits are reported in operating cash flows.
- Defined benefit, other postretirement, and postemployment plans: The company sponsors domestic and foreign defined benefit plans and provides certain severance/postemployment benefits. Obligations that vest or accumulate are recognized; non-vesting severance is expensed when incurred. Postemployment plans are unfunded. Funded status is recognized on the balance sheet, with changes recorded in AOCI.
- Use of estimates: Significant estimates affect revenue recognition, valuation of long-lived and intangible assets, redeemable interests, stock-based compensation, income taxes, and benefit plans; actual results may differ.
- New accounting standards adopted in fiscal 2020:

INTEREST RATE RISK

rate debt. Primary exposures include U.S. Treasury rates, LIBOR, Euribor, and commercial paper rates in the United States and Europe.
